title: Bent County, CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Bent County wells have a median depth of 80 ft and median yield of 15 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and water supply on your property.
h1: Water wells in Bent County, Colorado
intro_html:
Bent County sits on plains alluvium and sedimentary rock, and that shows up in the well records. Depths and yields are all over the map, but the overall picture is relatively shallow holes with solid production for household and stock use. Irrigation and monitoring wells round out a long drilling history here.

If you are looking at land around Las Animas, McClave, or Hasty, it helps to understand how deep most wells actually go, how much water they tend to make, and what that translates to in drilling and pump costs.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Bent County
sections.html:
Across Bent County, the median well depth is 80 feet, but the middle half of wells runs from 34 to 300 feet. That wide spread matters when you’re budgeting. A lot of holes stop shallow, but you also see plenty that push a few hundred feet before hitting reliable water.

About 52% of wells are under 100 feet, while roughly a quarter fall between 300 and 600 feet. Another 2% go deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest on record reaches 1,040 feet. A driller is going to price your job expecting something in that 34–300 foot band, but with a clear disclaimer that rock conditions and the specific aquifer could push you toward the deeper side.

Most permits list an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with smaller groups into the Dakota and Cheyenne units, so depth can change a lot over short distances.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water to expect
sections.html:
Where we do have pump tests reported, Bent County looks pretty favorable. The median reported yield is 15 gpm, and the middle half of wells comes in between 10 and 30 gpm. That’s plenty for a single household or stock well, and often enough to support some lawn or small-scale irrigation, subject to your permit limitations.

None of the reported wells fall under 1 gpm, and only 7% are in the 1–5 gpm band. About 35% land between 5 and 15 gpm, while 58% show 15 gpm or more. For a domestic or stock permit, those numbers suggest you’re more likely to be throttled by the legal pumping limit than by the well’s physical capacity.

Still, only 257 wells have yield data out of over 2,200 permits, so treat these as tendencies, not guarantees for your specific parcel.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they say about the table
sections.html:
Static water level data are sparse in Bent County, but what’s reported is useful. The median depth to water is 32 feet, with the middle half of readings from 14 down to 150 feet. In practice, that means some wells hit water almost at shallow trenching depth, while others need deeper pump settings and more lift.

With only 48 wells reporting static levels, we can’t draw a solid trend line over time from this dataset alone. However, the fact that a good share of wells are relatively shallow, while total depths often extend deeper, suggests drillers are chasing more productive zones below the first water they encounter.

When you evaluate a specific lot, pull nearby permits from Las Animas, McClave, or Hasty and look at both total depth and static level to get a better feel for the local water table.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling and when
sections.html:
Bent County has a long, steady drilling record. Permits begin to show up in the 1950s, with 56 that decade, then grow through 96 in the 1960s and 140 in the 1970s. Activity keeps building: 158 permits in the 1980s, 316 in the 1990s, then a peak of 493 in the 2000s.

Things taper off some in the 2010s with 216 permits and 78 so far in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. That mix tells you there are plenty of older wells around that may need inspection or rehabilitation, along with a good sample of modern completions.

Hoffman (Earl Hoffman) shows up as the most active driller with 312 wells, followed by Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 184 and Broce Drilling with 79. Local drillers will know the fractured-bedrock and alluvial conditions that dominate most of these records.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Bent County
sections.html:
The local drilling cost model for Bent County assumes alluvium over plains sedimentary rock, with a typical drilling rate of $35–$55 per foot. At the median 80-foot depth, the drilled hole alone usually runs about $2,800–$4,400.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a typical finished domestic or stock well at that depth pencils in around $8,800–$16,400. If your location or target aquifer pushes you into that 300–400 foot range, you can scale that by depth and expect a noticeable jump in both drilling and pump sizing costs.

When you get bids, have the driller quote by the foot with a clear allowance for hitting the deeper side of the local 34–300 foot middle range, not just the 80-foot median.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination, and siting
sections.html:
The county records don’t show a big cluster of sub-1 gpm wells, but yield data are limited, so you still need to plan for the chance of a marginal producer. In fractured-bedrock settings, two wells a few hundred yards apart can behave very differently.

The environmental mapping within about 10 miles flags 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 6 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup locations. Those don’t automatically mean your well is at risk, but they justify reviewing state and federal site data and considering water-quality testing once a well is online.

Siting also matters: keep enough separation from your septic system, barnyards, and chemical storage, and make sure the driller follows Colorado rules on casing and grout to keep shallow water and surface contamination out of the bore.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Bent County lot
sections.html:
Before you close on a parcel in Bent County, pull the surrounding well permits and look at actual depths and yields, especially near Las Animas, McClave, and Hasty where data are denser. Seeing neighbors mostly in the 34–300 foot depth band with 10–30 gpm yields is a good sign, but confirm details for your exact area.

If you’re buying an existing home, check whether the well is permitted for domestic or stock use and have the system inspected and flow-tested. For raw land, budget using the local $35–$55 per foot range and the 80-foot median, but keep cash reserves in case you end up in the deeper 300-foot territory.

Also confirm room for a compliant septic system, power routing to the pump, and access for a drill rig and service truck so you don’t find yourself with a well you can’t easily maintain.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Bent County, Colorado?
faq.a: Bent County wells have a median depth of 80 feet, but the middle half range from 34 to 300 feet. About 52% are under 100 feet, while roughly a quarter are 300–600 feet, and a small share go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest at 1,040 feet. Expect bids that plan for anything within that 34–300 foot band unless local data suggest otherwise.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Bent County, CO?
faq.a: Reported Bent County wells show a median yield of 15 gpm, with the middle half between 10 and 30 gpm. None of the reported wells are under 1 gpm, and most are above 5 gpm. That’s generally enough for household and stock use, subject to permit limits. Keep in mind that only 257 wells have reported yields, so check nearby permits for a more site-specific picture.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Bent County, Colorado?
faq.a: Local cost modeling for Bent County uses a drilling rate of about $35–$55 per foot in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 80-foot median depth, the hole alone usually runs $2,800–$4,400. A complete well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical typically totals around $8,800–$16,400 at that depth, with higher costs if your well must go significantly deeper.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Bent County, CO?
faq.a: The permit records don’t rate water quality, but mapped data show 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 6 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those are reasons to take water testing seriously. After drilling or when buying an existing well, budget for a lab test for bacteria, basic chemistry, and any contaminants of concern near your location.

faq.q: Are dry or low-producing wells common in Bent County?
faq.a: In the subset of wells with reported yields, none show less than 1 gpm, and the median is 15 gpm, which is encouraging. However, only 257 out of more than 2,200 permits report yield, and most wells tap fractured-bedrock or unnamed aquifers, which can be variable. When evaluating a property, look closely at nearby permits and talk with local drillers about any history of low-yield or problem holes in that specific area.
